exercise_group.instruction: In Exercises 5–8, determine if the columns of the matrix form a linearly independent set. Justify each answer.

exercise_group.instruction: In Exercises 21–28, mark each statement True or False (T/F). Justify each answer on the basis of a careful reading of the text.

problem.paragraph: (T/F) The columns of a matrix $$A$$ are linearly independent if the equation $$A{\mathbf{x} = 0}$$ has the trivial solution.
(T/F) Two vectors are linearly dependent if and only if they lie on a line through the origin.
(T/F) If $$S$$ is a linearly dependent set, then each vector is a linear combination of the other vectors in $$S$$ .
(T/F) If a set contains fewer vectors than there are entries in the vectors, then the set is linearly independent.
(T/F) The columns of any $$4 \times 5$$ matrix are linearly dependent.

(T/F) If $$\mathbf{x}$$ and $$\mathbf{y}$$ are linearly independent, and if $$\mathbf{z}$$ is in $$\text{Span\{} \mathbf{x} \text{,} \mathbf{y} \text{\}}$$ , then $$\{\mathbf{x} \text{,} \mathbf{y} \text{,} \mathbf{z}\}$$ is linearly dependent.

(T/F) If $$\mathbf{x}$$ and $$\mathbf{y}$$ are linearly independent, and if $$\{\mathbf{x} \text{,} \mathbf{y} \text{,} \mathbf{z}\}$$ is linearly dependent, then $$\mathbf{z}$$ is in $$\text{Span} \{\mathbf{x} \text{,} \mathbf{y}\}$$ .
(T/F) If a set in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ is linearly dependent, then the set contains more vectors than there are entries in each vector.

exercise_group.instruction: In Exercises 29–32, describe the possible echelon forms of the matrix. Use the notation of Example 1 in Section 1.2.

problem.paragraph: $$A$$ is a $$3 \times 3$$ matrix with linearly independent columns.
$$A$$ is a $$2 \times 2$$ matrix with linearly dependent columns.
$$A$$ is a $$4 \times 2$$ matrix, $$A = \lbrack\mathbf{a}_{1} \mathbf{a}_{2}\rbrack$$ , and $$\mathbf{a}_{2}$$ is not a multiple of $$\mathbf{a}_{1}$$ .

$$A$$ is a $$4 \times 3$$ matrix, $$A = \lbrack\mathbf{a}_{1} \mathbf{a}_{2} \mathbf{a}_{3}\rbrack$$ , such that $$\left\{ \mathbf{a}_{1} \text{,} \mathbf{a}_{2} \right\}$$ is linearly independent and $$\mathbf{a}_{3}$$ is not in $$\text{Span\{} \mathbf{a}_{1} \text{,} \mathbf{a}_{2} \text{\}}$$ .
How many pivot columns must a $$7 \times 5$$ matrix have if its columns are linearly independent? Why?
How many pivot columns must a $$5 \times 7$$ matrix have if its columns span $$\mathbb{R}^{5} \text{?}$$ Why?
Construct $$3 \times 2$$ matrices $$A$$ and $$B$$ such that $$A\mathbf{x} = 0$$ has only the trivial solution and $$B\mathbf{x} = 0$$ has a nontrivial solution.

list.item: Fill in the blank in the following statement: “If $$A$$ is an $$m \times n$$ matrix, then the columns of $$A$$ are linearly independent if and only if $$A$$ has _______ pivot columns.”
Explain why the statement in (a) is true.

exercise_group.instruction: Exercises 37 and 38 should be solved without performing row operations. [Hint: Write $$A\mathbf{x} = 0$$ as a vector equation.]

problem.paragraph: Given $$A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 & 5 \\ {- 5} & 1 & {- 4} \\ {- 3} & {- 1} & {- 4} \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$$ , observe that the third column is the sum of the first two columns. Find a nontrivial solution of $$A\mathbf{x} = 0$$ .

Given $$A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 1 & 6 \\ {- 7} & 5 & 3 \\ 9 & {- 3} & 3 \end{bmatrix}$$ , observe that the first column plus twice the second column equals the third column. Find a nontrivial solution of $$A\mathbf{x} = 0$$ .

exercise_group.instruction: Each statement in Exercises 39–44 is either true (in all cases) or false (for at least one example). If false, construct a specific example to show that the statement is not always true. Such an example is called a counterexample to the statement. If a statement is true, give a justification. (One specific example cannot explain why a statement is always true. You will have to do more work here than in Exercises 21–28.)

problem.paragraph: (T/F-C) If $$\mathbf{v}_{1} \text{,…,} \mathbf{v}_{4}$$ are in $$\mathbb{R}^{4}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}_{3} = 2\mathbf{v}_{1} + \mathbf{v}_{2}$$ , then $$\{\mathbf{v}_{1} \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{2} \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{3} \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{4}\}$$ is linearly dependent.

(T/F-C) If $$\mathbf{v}_{1} \text{,…,} \mathbf{v}_{4}$$ are in $$\mathbb{R}^{4}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}_{3} = 0$$ , then $$\{\mathbf{v}_{1} \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{2} \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{3} \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{4}\}$$ is linearly dependent.

(T/F-C) If $$\mathbf{v}_{1}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}_{2}$$ are in $$\mathbb{R}^{4}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}_{2}$$ is not a scalar multiple of $$\mathbf{v}_{1}$$ , then $$\{\mathbf{v}_{1} \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{2}\}$$ is linearly independent.

(T/F-C) If $$\mathbf{v}_{1} \text{,…,} \mathbf{v}_{4}$$ are in $$\mathbb{R}^{4}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}_{3}$$ is not a linear combination of $$\mathbf{v}_{1} \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{2} \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{4}$$ , then $$\{\mathbf{v}_{1} \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{2} \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{3} \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{4}\}$$ is linearly independent.

(T/F-C) If $$\mathbf{v}_{1} \text{,…,} \mathbf{v}_{4}$$ are in $$\mathbb{R}^{4}$$ and $$\{\mathbf{v}_{1} \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{2} \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{3}\}$$ is linearly dependent, then $$\{\mathbf{v}_{1} \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{2} \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{3} \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{4}\}$$ is also linearly dependent.

(T/F-C) If $$\mathbf{v}_{1} \text{,…,} \mathbf{v}_{4}$$ are linearly independent vectors in $$\mathbb{R}^{4}$$ , then $$\{\mathbf{v}_{1} \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{2} \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{3}\}$$ is also linearly independent. [Hint: Think about $$x_{1}\mathbf{v}_{1} + x_{2}\mathbf{v}_{2} + x_{3}\mathbf{v}_{3} + 0 \cdot \mathbf{v}_{4} = 0$$ .]

Suppose $$A$$ is an $$m \times n$$ matrix with the property that for all $$\mathbf{b}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{m}$$ the equation $$A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$$ has at most one solution. Use the definition of linear independence to explain why the columns of $$A$$ must be linearly independent.

Suppose an $$m \times n$$ matrix $$A$$ has $$n$$ pivot columns. Explain why for each $$\mathbf{b}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{m}$$ the equation $$A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$$ has at most one solution. [Hint: Explain why $$A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$$ cannot have infinitely many solutions.]

exercise_group.instruction: [T] In Exercises 47 and 48, use as many columns of $$A$$ as possible to construct a matrix $$B$$ with the property that the equation $$B\mathbf{x} = 0$$ has only the trivial solution. Solve $$B\mathbf{x} = 0$$ to verify your work.

problem.paragraph: [T] With $$A$$ and $$B$$ as in Exercise 47 select a column $$\mathbf{v}$$ of $$A$$ that was not used in the construction of $$B$$ and determine if $$\mathbf{v}$$ is in the set spanned by the columns of $$B$$ . (Describe your calculations.)
[T] Repeat Exercise 49 with the matrices $$A$$ and $$B$$ from Exercise 48. Then give an explanation for what you discover, assuming that $$B$$ was constructed as specified.

No. When testing for linear independence, it is usually a poor idea to check if one selected vector is a linear combination of the others. It may happen that the selected vector is not a linear combination of the others and yet the whole set of vectors is linearly dependent. In this practice problem, $$\mathbf{w}$$ is not a linear combination of $$\mathbf{u}$$ , $$\mathbf{v}$$ , and $$\mathbf{z}$$ .

problem.paragraph: Applying the definition of linearly dependent to $$\left\{ \mathbf{v}_{1} \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{2} \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{3} \right\}$$ implies that there exist scalars $$c_{1}$$ , $$c_{2}$$ , and $$c_{3}$$ , not all zero, such that $$c_{1} \mathbf{v}_{1} + c_{2} \mathbf{v}_{2} + c_{3} \mathbf{v}_{3} = 0 .$$
Adding $$0\mathbf{v}_{4} = 0$$ to both sides of this equation results in $$c_{1} \mathbf{v}_{1} + c_{2} \mathbf{v}_{2} + c_{3} \mathbf{v}_{3} + 0 \mathbf{v}_{4} = 0 .$$

Since $$c_{1} \text{,} c_{2} \text{,} c_{3}$$ and $$0$$ are not all zero, the set $$\left\{ \mathbf{v}_{1} \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{2} \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{3} \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{4} \right\}$$ satisfies the definition of a linearly dependent set.
